newsitem.title: USA: Court rules against Los Angeles redevelopment plan.
newsitem.headline: Court rules against Los Angeles redevelopment plan.

text.p: A California court on Wednesday shot down Los Angeles' plan to lift a redevelopment agency's $750 million spending cap in a decision that could scuttle billions of dollars of bond issues, attorneys said.

The 2nd District Court of Appeal in Los Angeles affirmed the judgment of the trial court, which held in 1995 that it lacked jurisdiction to modify the cap or debt limit for the so-called Central Business District Redevelopment Project.
Attorneys opposed to the city's plan hailed the ruling, saying it could block billions of dollars of future redevelopment borrowings.

"This was not (bond) money that would go to police, fire, libraries and public health. This was money for developers. This was money to develop real estate," lead plaintiffs' attorney Barbara Blinderman said.
City attorneys were not immediately available to comment.

The Los Angeles redevelopment controversy began more than 20 years ago. In July 1975, the Los Angeles City Council approved a redevelopment plan for the Central Business District Redevelopment Project.
The project included more than 1,500 acres of downtown Los Angeles which the city council had deemed to be in a "blighted" condition.

In September 1975, Ernani Bernardi, a member of the city council, challenged the redevelopment plan. He argued that the plan was too expensive and that the redevelopment funds would not provide enough of a benefit to the public.

Two years later Bernardi, the city, the Community Redevelopment Agency (CRA) and several other local entities resolved the dispute, entering into a so-called "stipulated judgment" that imposed fiscal restrictions on the project.
Under the terms of the 1977 stipulated judgment, the CRA could not receive more than $750 million from tax increment funds for use in connection with the project.
The judgment also said the CRA could not incur any debt repayable from tax increments in connection with the project at any time after July 19, 1995.
"They (Bernardi and his supporters) thought $750 million was an enormous amount of money. Nobody ever thought they'd be able to spend that much," Blinderman said.

But in 1986, the CRA proposed raising the tax increment spending limit from $750 million to $7.1 billion. The CRA also proposed extending the debt time limit from July 1995 to July 2010. The city adopted the proposal.
